title: How does Flink achieve end-to-end exactly-once semantics (checkpointed state + a two-phase-commit sink via TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction to Kafka/JDBC/Iceberg — pre-commit on checkpoint, commit on checkpoint-complete)?
shortTitle: How does Flink achieve end-to-end exactly-once

s1_definition.profdef: End-to-end exactly-once in Flink means that each input record affects the final external output exactly once, even across failures, combining two mechanisms. First, Flink's barrier-based checkpointing gives exactly-once state consistency internally, so operator state reflects each record once. Second, for the external sink, Flink uses a transactional two-phase commit protocol, historically via TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction and now via the unified Sink API, where the sink pre-commits its output as part of a checkpoint and only finally commits that transaction when the checkpoint is confirmed complete. Because the commit is tied to checkpoint completion, a failure before completion rolls back the pending transaction, so no partial or duplicate output ever becomes visible externally.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to guarantee that every transaction is written to the external ledger exactly once, never zero times and never twice, even if a server crashes mid-write. The trick is a two-stage signature. When the clerk reaches a checkpoint, they prepare the ledger entries but leave them in a sealed envelope that is not yet filed; this is the pre-commit. Only once the bank's head office confirms that the whole checkpoint across all clerks succeeded does the clerk open the envelope and file the entries for real; this is the commit. If a crash happens before head office confirms, the sealed envelope is simply torn up and nothing was filed, so recovery re-does the work from the last good checkpoint without any double entries. The external ledger therefore sees each transaction exactly once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flink gets exactly-once end to end by pairing checkpointed state with a sink that pre-commits on checkpoint and only commits when the checkpoint completes, so failures roll back uncommitted output.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** End-to-end exactly-once in Flink means that each input record affects the final external output exactly once, even across failures, combining two mechanisms. First, Flink's barrier-based checkpointing gives exactly-once state consistency internally, so operator state reflects each record once. Second, for the external sink, Flink uses a transactional two-phase commit protocol, historically via TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction and now via the unified Sink API, where the sink pre-commits its output as part of a checkpoint and only finally commits that transaction when the checkpoint is confirmed complete. Because the commit is tied to checkpoint completion, a failure before completion rolls back the pending transaction, so no partial or duplicate output ever becomes visible externally.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to guarantee that every transaction is written to the external ledger exactly once, never zero times and never twice, even if a server crashes mid-write. The trick is a two-stage signature. When the clerk reaches a checkpoint, they prepare the ledger entries but leave them in a sealed envelope that is not yet filed; this is the pre-commit. Only once the bank's head office confirms that the whole checkpoint across all clerks succeeded does the clerk open the envelope and file the entries for real; this is the commit. If a crash happens before head office confirms, the sealed envelope is simply torn up and nothing was filed, so recovery re-does the work from the last good checkpoint without any double entries. The external ledger therefore sees each transaction exactly once.

**One line to remember:** Flink gets exactly-once end to end by pairing checkpointed state with a sink that pre-commits on checkpoint and only commits when the checkpoint completes, so failures roll back uncommitted output.

sections.s2_technical:
Internally, exactly-once state is guaranteed by checkpointing. Barriers flow through the graph, operators snapshot a consistent cut, sources record their offsets in the checkpoint, and on recovery Flink restores state and rewinds sources so each record updates state exactly once. But internal consistency is not enough: the sink writes to the outside world, and the outside world does not automatically roll back when Flink recovers. If the sink naively wrote output as it processed and then the job failed and replayed, the replayed records would be written again, producing duplicates. So the sink must participate in the checkpoint using a transactional protocol.

The two-phase commit protocol ties the external transaction's lifecycle to the checkpoint lifecycle. It has four hooks, classically in TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction. `beginTransaction` starts a new external transaction when a checkpoint interval begins, for example opening a Kafka transaction or a JDBC transaction. `preCommit` is called when the checkpoint barrier reaches the sink: the sink flushes its buffered output into the open transaction and prepares it to commit, but does not commit yet, and this pending state is stored in the checkpoint so it can be recovered. `commit` is called only after the JobManager confirms the checkpoint is globally complete; at that point the sink commits the transaction, making the output visible. `abort` is called to roll back a transaction that will not be committed, for example on failure. Because the actual commit happens only on checkpoint completion, which is the single moment the whole job agrees it reached a consistent state, any failure before that completion leaves the transaction uncommitted, and recovery either aborts it or, for idempotent commit targets, safely re-commits the recovered pending transaction.

Different sinks realize this differently. A Kafka sink uses Kafka's transactions and transactional producer so that pre-committed records are invisible to consumers reading in read-committed mode until the commit lands. A JDBC sink can use XA transactions. An Iceberg or Delta sink stages data files and only commits the table metadata pointing to them on checkpoint completion. The senior nuances are important. There is a visibility latency: downstream readers only see output after the checkpoint completes, so the checkpoint interval becomes the end-to-end latency floor for exactly-once output. You must configure the Kafka transaction timeout to be larger than your maximum checkpoint interval plus recovery time, otherwise transactions expire and you lose data. If the external system cannot do transactions, you can instead achieve effectively-once with an idempotent sink keyed by a deterministic id, where replays overwrite rather than duplicate. And exactly-once is a contract across the whole pipeline: a source that cannot replay, or a sink that cannot transact or deduplicate, breaks it regardless of Flink's internal guarantees.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India streams settled transactions into an external ledger topic that downstream accounting systems consume. It is absolutely unacceptable to write a settlement twice, because that would double-count money, or to lose one, because the ledger would not balance. If the Flink job crashes after writing some output but before the checkpoint completes, a naive sink would replay and duplicate those writes. This is exactly why a two-phase-commit sink is required: output is pre-committed but invisible until the checkpoint completes, so a crash rolls it back cleanly.

Problem 2 — The accounting consumers must never see a half-written batch or a record that later gets rolled back. They should only ever read fully committed, checkpoint-confirmed output. This is exactly the read-committed visibility behavior of the transactional sink: consumers see records only after the commit that follows checkpoint completion.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo reproducing the two-phase commit lifecycle. We define a `Settlement` record. A `TransactionalLedgerSink` mimics TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction with beginTransaction, preCommit, commit, and abort, writing into a pending buffer that only becomes visible in a committed store on commit. A `CheckpointDriver` drives the lifecycle: begin a transaction, process records into it, pre-commit when a barrier arrives, and commit only when the checkpoint is confirmed complete, with the ability to simulate a crash between pre-commit and commit to show rollback. An `ExactlyOnceDemo` main class processes settlements, shows a successful checkpoint committing output exactly once, then shows a crash after pre-commit that aborts and replays without duplicating, verifying the committed store has each settlement exactly once.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  exactly-once:
    checkpoint-interval-ms: 10000
    kafka:
      transaction-timeout-ms: 900000   # MUST exceed max checkpoint+recovery
      isolation: read_committed
    sink: kafka                         # kafka | jdbc-xa | iceberg
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two settlement batches. Batch one has two settlements for Rajesh and Priya; batch two has one settlement for Rajesh, which will experience a crash after pre-commit.

Step 1: The clean checkpoint cycle begins a transaction and writes both batch-one settlements into the pending buffer. At this point the records exist only inside the open transaction and are not visible to any downstream consumer.

Step 2: The checkpoint barrier reaches the sink, triggering pre-commit. The sink flushes the two records into the transaction and prepares it, storing the pending state in the checkpoint, but it still does not commit, so the records remain invisible.

Step 3: The JobManager confirms the checkpoint is globally complete, and only then is commit called. The two settlements become visible in the committed ledger exactly once. Downstream accounting consumers reading in read-committed mode now see them.

Step 4: The crash scenario begins. A transaction is opened and the single batch-two settlement is written into the pending buffer, then pre-commit is called, flushing it into the transaction and making it checkpoint-recoverable but still invisible.

Step 5: A crash is simulated after pre-commit but before the checkpoint is confirmed. Because the commit never happened, the sink aborts, discarding the uncommitted transaction. Crucially, the batch-two settlement was never made visible, so there is nothing to duplicate.

Step 6: Recovery replays from the last completed checkpoint. Flink rewinds the source and re-processes the same batch-two settlement into a fresh transaction, pre-commits, and this time the checkpoint completes so it commits. Because the first attempt was aborted, the settlement is now committed exactly once. The final committed ledger contains three distinct settlement ids, each exactly once, proving end-to-end exactly-once despite the crash.

```
  Settlement records
    │

  Flink job (checkpointed state = exactly-once internally)
    │ barrier reaches sink
    ▼
  TransactionalLedgerSink (TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction)
    │ beginTransaction
    │ write → PENDING buffer (invisible)

    │
    ├─ checkpoint COMPLETE confirmed ──→ commit ──→ VISIBLE (exactly once)

  Accounting consumers (read_committed) see each settlement exactly once
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
End-to-end exactly-once in Flink means every input record affects the final external output exactly once, even across failures, and it is achieved by combining two distinct mechanisms. The first is Flink's barrier-based checkpointing, which gives exactly-once state consistency internally: barriers flow through the graph, operators snapshot a consistent cut, sources record their offsets, and on recovery Flink restores state and rewinds the sources so each record updates state exactly once. But internal consistency alone is not enough, because the sink writes to the outside world, and the outside world does not roll itself back when Flink recovers. If a sink wrote output as it processed and the job then failed and replayed, the replayed records would be written again and you would get duplicates. So the sink must participate in the checkpoint through a transactional protocol.

That protocol is two-phase commit, historically implemented through TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction and now through the unified Sink API, and it has four hooks tied to the checkpoint lifecycle. beginTransaction opens a new external transaction when a checkpoint interval starts. preCommit runs when the checkpoint barrier reaches the sink: it flushes the buffered output into the transaction and prepares it, storing the pending state in the checkpoint, but it does not commit. commit runs only after the JobManager confirms the checkpoint is globally complete, and only then does the output become visible. abort rolls back a transaction that will not be committed. Because the real commit happens only on checkpoint completion, any failure before that leaves the transaction uncommitted, so recovery either aborts it or safely re-commits the recovered pending transaction, and no partial or duplicate output ever becomes externally visible. A Kafka sink implements this with Kafka transactions so pre-committed records are invisible to read-committed consumers until commit, a JDBC sink can use XA, and an Iceberg or Delta sink stages files and commits the table metadata on completion. The key senior points are that there is a visibility latency equal to the checkpoint interval, that the Kafka transaction timeout must exceed your maximum checkpoint plus recovery time or you lose data, and that if the sink cannot transact you fall back to effectively-once with idempotent writes keyed by a deterministic id.

At the National Bank of India we used exactly this for our settlement ledger pipeline. We ran the job in exactly-once mode with checkpointed keyed state and a transactional Kafka sink with a transactional id prefix, and the accounting consumers read in read-committed mode so they only ever saw settlements after the commit that followed checkpoint completion, never a half-written or rolled-back batch. I could demonstrate the guarantee concretely: a clean checkpoint committed its settlements exactly once, and when I simulated a crash after pre-commit but before the checkpoint confirmed, the sink aborted the uncommitted transaction, recovery replayed the same settlements, and they ended up committed exactly once with no duplicate. We also carefully set the Kafka transaction timeout well above our checkpoint interval plus recovery budget, and we used deterministic settlement ids so that even our idempotent paths could not double-count. Being able to explain that exactly-once is the pairing of checkpointed state with a two-phase-commit sink, walk through begin, preCommit, commit, and abort, and call out the visibility latency and the transaction-timeout pitfall is exactly what proves you have run a financial-grade Flink pipeline.
